extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners in crisis communication / public relations (general Wikipedia readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of William Benoit's image restoration (image repair) theory: a typology of strategies organizations or individuals can use to restore reputation after an offense, plus factors and case-based recommendations for choosing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for engaging image restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Two components must be present in a given attack to the image of an individual or organization: The accused is held responsible for an action. the act is considered offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two conditions indicate when an actor will consider an image-restorative response; if either is absent (no perceived responsibility or not offensive), defensive strategies are unlikely to be necessary or effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical assumptions guiding image restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Image restoration theory is grounded in two fundamental assumptions. Communication is a goal-directed activity. ... Maintaining a favorable reputation is a key goal of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should assume communicators will prioritize goals (often reputation), weigh trade-offs, and select defensive strategies that best serve their most important goals at reasonable cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image repair factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Some image repair factors include Crisis responsibility – how much a company or person is responsible for in a crisis; Crisis type – what type of crisis is happening; Organizational reputation – what is the known reputation and behavior of a company or a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors influence which strategy will be effective: greater responsibility typically requires stronger remedial responses; crisis type and prior reputation moderate audience reaction and strategy efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual and situational criteria for choosing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception is fundamental to image restoration, as the accused actor will not engage in a defensive strategy unless the perception exists that he is at fault. The actor who committed the wrongful act must decide on the strategy of the best course based on their specific situation. Factors such as credibility, audience perceptions, and the degree of offensiveness of the act must be taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision criteria include perceived culpability, actor credibility (trustworthiness), audience characteristics and expectations, and how offensive/serious the act is; practitioners must weigh these when selecting among strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial — The accused may simply deny that the act occurred, or shift the blame to the 'real' culprit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when evidence supports non-involvement or when innocence is credible. Case examples: Benoit notes denial used effectively when an organization/person is actually innocent. Risk: if evidence later contradicts denial, reputational damage may increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evading responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evading responsibility — When unable to deny performing the act in question, the accused may attempt to evade responsibility. This strategy has four components: Provocation: the actor may claim that the act was committed in response to another wrongful act. Defeasibility: the actor pleads a lack of knowledge or control over important factors related to the offensive act. Unaccountability: the actor may make an excuse for factors beyond their control. Bona fide: the actor asks not to be held fully responsible based on their good, rather than evil motives in committing the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evading responsibility is appropriate when outright denial is impossible; each subcomponent offers a different justificatory frame. These tactics can reduce perceived culpability but may fail if audiences reject the excuse or see it as shirking responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing offensiveness of the act
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing offensiveness — The accused may attempt to reduce the degree of negative feeling experienced by the audience. This strategy has six components: Bolstering: used to mitigate the negative effects by reinforcing the audience's positive idea of the accused. They may remind the audience of prior good acts. Minimization: attempts to convince the audience that the act in question is less serious than it appears. Differentiation: the act is distinguished from other, more offensive acts in order to lessen the audience's negative sentiment by means of comparison. Transcendence: the act is placed in a broad context to place it in a different, less offensive frame of reference. Ad hominem: the actor attacks their accusers or questions the credibility of the sources of the accusations. Compensation: the actor offers to redress the victims of their action in order to offset the negative sentiment that is being held against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing offensiveness offers multiple tactics to reframe or soften perceptions. Bolstering (reminding of prior good acts) is highlighted as often effective. Risks include appearing manipulative or shifting blame unfairly (ad hominem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrective action — The accused claims that they will correct the problem. This can involve restoring the situation to its prior state, or promising to make changes to prevent its reoccurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended when the organization is at fault and can take concrete steps; must be publicized to restore trust. Effective corrective action often needs clear commitments, timelines, and demonstrated follow-through to be credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortification
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortification — The accused admits responsibility and asks for forgiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mortification (apology and acceptance of responsibility) is a strong remedial strategy when guilt is clear. It should be sincere and often combined with corrective action. Benoit's cases emphasize mortification as a dominant recommended response in many guilty scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benoit's case-study recommendations (prescriptive guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on several case studies by Benoit and his colleagues, a number of prescriptive recommendations were cited for the use of crisis strategies: The dominant recommendation is for an organization to immediately admit fault/accept responsibility. Corrective actions should be taken and an organization need to publicize those actions. Bolstering, which is directly related to the charge, is the most effective strategy. If the organization is innocent, denial is an effective strategy. 'Image restoration theory is the dominant line of research generating these recommendations. The most common recommendations suggest using the mortification and corrective action crisis response when an organization is guilty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are empirically derived, case-based recommendations. They emphasize immediacy, publicized remediation, and bolstering; however, their applicability depends on context and accuracy of responsibility attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical limitations and cautions (Coombs' critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation of Image repair theory – Coombs: ...his studies using situational crisis communication theory found no support for always using mortification and corrective action. Also, the mortification and corrective action strategies had no greater effect than a simple bolstering strategy in a criminal violation crisis such as racial discrimination (Coombs, 2006). This theory can not be predicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should not treat Benoit's prescriptions as one-size-fits-all; situational analyses and larger-sample empirical studies may show different effective strategies. Caution against overgeneralizing from limited case-study evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice from comparative advertising analysis (Cola Wars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benoit analyses advertisements from both companies from 1990–1992 ... He advises that companies should avoid making false claims, provide adequate support for claims, and develop themes throughout a campaign, and avoid arguments that might backfire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding in advertising or campaign contexts, avoid inflammatory or unsupported claims; build consistent themes and evidence; anticipate potential backfire effects before deploying an image-restoration message.
